items.title: The challenge is more productive employment
items.syllabus: GS3 › Inclusive growth; Employment; Growth and development · GS1 › Poverty; Role of women; Migration · GS2 › Issues relating to poverty
items.summary: With extreme poverty down to 2.6%, the editorial argues the next obstacle to mass prosperity is the lack of productive, better-paid non-farm jobs.
evolution: World Bank: extreme poverty falls to 2.6% in 2023; poverty concentrated in the UP–West Bengal belt (front page).
Manish Sabharwal: 'Challenge is wages, not jobs' (editorial page).
Editorial: the challenge is more productive employment.
ideas: Poverty fell, productivity did not follow: extreme poverty is down to 2.6% and the $4.2 line to 16.1%, but the lack of productive, better-paid non-farm jobs now blocks mass prosperity.
GS3 · Inclusive growth
India's next development challenge is not poverty reduction alone but productive employment.
More workers, not better work: labour force participation has risen, mostly as women join, but many are in farming or self-employment.
GS3 · Employment / GS1 · Women
Rising participation driven by women in farm and self-employment adds workers without raising productivity.
Stalled structural transformation: agriculture still employs a large share of workers compared with China and Vietnam, and most non-farm workers are in informal, low-productivity firms.
GS3 · Structural transformation
India's workforce has not moved out of farming at the pace East Asian economies managed.
Manufacturing missed its role: unlike other Asian economies, Indian manufacturing has not absorbed low-skilled workers; jobs grew in low-end services instead.
GS3 · Industrial policy
Without labour-intensive manufacturing, workers leaving farms crowd into low-end services.
Geography of jobs: poverty is concentrated in the UP–West Bengal belt, where incomes and jobs are scarce, so migration to richer regions is the main route to non-farm work.
GS1 · Migration / Regional disparity
Regional job deserts make migration the default escape route from poverty.
keywords: Shift of workers from low- to high-productivity sectors
Moving up the income ladder requires structural transformation of the workforce.
Manufacturing peaking early, before absorbing surplus labour
India shows signs of premature deindustrialisation, with services absorbing low-skilled labour.
Growth stalling before reaching high income
Low-productivity jobs risk trapping India below upper-middle income.
Moving for work because local options are absent
Job scarcity in the eastern belt drives distress migration.
Industries employing many low-skilled workers per unit of capital
Labour-intensive manufacturing is the missing bridge from farm to formal work.
data: Extreme poverty ($3/day) and poverty at the $4.2 lower-middle-income line (from 57.7% in 2011)
World Bank, via IE
GS1 · Poverty
Extreme poverty fell to 2.6% in 2023, and the $4.2-line rate fell from 57.7% to 16.1% (World Bank).
Labour force participation rate, ages 15+
Periodic Labour Force Survey, via IE
GS3 · Employment
India's labour force participation rose to about 59% in 2025 (PLFS), mainly as women joined.
Share of workers in agriculture in China and Vietnam
World Bank, via IE
GS3 · Structural transformation
Only 21.68% of China's and 25% of Vietnam's workers are in agriculture (World Bank), far below India.
Share of India's poor in the belt from UP to West Bengal
World Bank, via IE
GS1 · Regional disparity
57% of India's poor live in the UP–West Bengal belt (World Bank).
examples: China and Vietnam's farm-to-factory shift
Smaller farm workforces after manufacturing absorbed labour
GS3 · Structural transformation · GS1 · Globalisation
China and Vietnam show how labour-intensive manufacturing moves workers out of farming.
UP–West Bengal poverty belt
Low incomes, few jobs, migration as the outlet
GS1 · Migration, regional disparity · GS3 · Inclusive growth
The UP–West Bengal belt shows why place-based job creation is central to ending poverty.
pyqs: Labour-led growth and job creation without hurting productivity.
Why manufacturing failed at labour-intensive exports.

trend.t: Employment questions moved from informalisation (2016) and labour-intensive exports (2017) to labour-led growth without losing productivity (2022) and structural unemployment (2023). Inclusive growth recurs almost every year in GS3.
trend.watch: Job quality, not job numbers, is the thread across 2016–2023. Prepare structural transformation: farm to manufacturing, informality and regional disparity.

potential: "India's challenge is no longer poverty but productivity." Discuss. (15 marks)
Why has Indian manufacturing failed to absorb low-skilled labour? Suggest measures. (10 marks)

practice.q: Why has Indian manufacturing failed to absorb low-skilled labour? Suggest measures.

answer.t: Extreme poverty is down to 2.6% (World Bank), yet only 21.68% of China's and 25% of Vietnam's workers are in farming, far below India, because Indian manufacturing has not absorbed surplus labour.

pts.t: Growth in capital- and skill-intensive industries.
Compliance burden discourages scale and formal hiring.
Most enterprises stay small and low-productivity.
Raise the cost of labour-intensive exports.
Workers lack industry-ready skills.
Jobs far from the eastern belt where labour is.
Textiles, footwear, food processing, electronics assembly.
Ease compliance so firms grow and formalise.
Industrial parks in UP, Bihar and Bengal.
Apprenticeships tied to factory demand.

answer.t: Moving workers from farm to factory is the bridge from poverty reduction to mass prosperity.

items.title: Smaller cities can lead the way on climate resilience
items.where: The Ideas Page, page 11 (Vaishnavi T G Shankar, Vasudha Foundation & Sanjay Sridhar)
items.syllabus: GS1 › Urbanisation, its problems and remedies · GS3 › Climate change; Disaster management; Conservation · GS2 › Local self-government (urban local bodies)
items.summary: The writers argue that heat and floods in cities stem from the same planning decisions, and that smaller cities, still growing, can build climate resilience into how they expand.
ideas: One root, two hazards: urban heat and flooding are shaped by the same decisions on land, buildings and infrastructure, yet are handled separately; the IPCC's 'climate-resilient development' joins adaptation, emissions cuts and development.
GS3 · Climate change / GS1 · Urbanisation
Heat and floods in Indian cities share a root in land use and building design, so they need one integrated plan.

Frameworks exist, practice lags: India's long-term low-emissions strategy (UNFCCC), the National Mission on Sustainable Habitat, the Urban Flood Risk Management Programme and heat's status as a notified disaster must now enter routine planning and investment.
GS3 · Disaster management / Climate policy
Recognising heat as a notified disaster opens disaster funds for heat resilience; the next step is routine planning.

Smaller cities can shape growth, not retrofit it: much of urban India and its future housing are in cities still expanding, where today's decisions on roads, drainage and buildings can lock in either vulnerability or resilience.
GS1 · Urbanisation
Smaller cities can avoid the costly retrofits of metros by building resilience into how they grow.
Cooling is a planning question: land use, density, expansion and green cover shape cooling demand; building design and efficiency can cut it substantially.
GS3 · Energy / Climate
Urban form, not just temperature, decides how much cooling a city needs.

Coordination and smart money: master plans, roads, utilities and building rules sit in separate departments; climate must enter project appraisal, existing budgets and grants, with CSR and development finance for pilots and local knowledge guiding data.
GS2 · Urban governance
Climate resilience in cities needs inter-departmental coordination more than new funding streams.
keywords: IPCC idea joining adaptation, mitigation and development
Climate-resilient development treats heat, floods and growth as one planning problem.
Cities hotter than surroundings due to built surfaces
Dense, grey urban form intensifies the urban heat island.
Early infrastructure choices fixing long-term outcomes
Roads and drainage built today create climate lock-in for decades.
Building climate into routine plans and budgets
Mainstreaming climate into master plans matters more than standalone projects.
Notifying heat as a disaster lets states use disaster funds for heat action.
data: Possible cut in cooling demand through building design, energy efficiency and thermal comfort practices
India Cooling Action Plan, via IE
GS3 · Energy / Climate
The India Cooling Action Plan estimates better building design and efficiency could cut cooling demand by 20% by 2037-38.
examples: Heat notified as a disaster
Disaster funds can now be used for heat resilience
GS3 · Disaster management · GS2 · Governance innovation
Notifying heat as a disaster shows policy adapting to new climate risks.
Urban Flood Risk Management Programme
Covers 18 cities
GS1 · Urban floods · GS3 · Disaster management
The Urban Flood Risk Management Programme marks a shift from flood relief to flood-risk planning in cities.
pyqs: Flooding of million cities, including smart ones, and remedies.
Urban flooding as a climate-induced disaster and the policy frameworks.
Infrastructure development vs disaster-risk reduction in sensitive areas.

trend.t: Urban questions moved from social problems of urbanisation (2013) and smart cities (2015, 2016, 2025) to urban floods (2016, 2020, GS3 2024) and Tier 2 cities (2022). Climate-linked urban risk is now asked in GS1 and GS3, and the infrastructure–disaster trade-off came in 2026.
trend.watch: Urban flooding has been asked in 2016, 2020 and 2024. Expect heat and smaller cities next: prepare integrated urban climate planning with examples.
focus: Urban floods and heat as linked climate risks
Disaster funds and frameworks for cities

potential: "Smaller cities offer India its best chance to build climate resilience into urbanisation." Discuss. (15 marks)
Why should urban heat and urban flooding be addressed together? Suggest planning measures. (10 marks)

practice.q: Why should urban heat and urban flooding be addressed together? Suggest planning measures.

answer.t: Indian cities face heat and floods every season; India has notified heat as a disaster and runs an Urban Flood Risk Management Programme in 18 cities, yet the two are planned separately.

pts.t: Concrete cover, lost wetlands and poor drainage worsen both.
Green cover and water bodies cool cities and absorb rain.
Master plans, roads and building rules shape both risks.
Heat raises cooling demand and power use.
Informal settlements suffer both.
Climate risk in zoning and project appraisal.
Protect lakes, wetlands and tree cover.
Cool roofs and passive design.
pts.ex: India Cooling Action Plan: 20% cut in cooling demand by 2037-38.

pts.t: Development authorities, public works and municipalities plan jointly.
Plan growth before it locks in.

answer.t: One plan for heat and floods, made early in smaller cities, is cheaper and safer than two crises handled late.

items.title: Misri to visit Nepal tomorrow, set stage for Balen's likely trip to India this month
items.syllabus: GS2 › India and its neighbourhood; Bilateral agreements · GS3 › Infrastructure: energy (hydropower), connectivity; Disaster management
items.summary: Foreign Secretary Misri visits Nepal to prepare for PM Balen Shah's likely India visit, with connectivity, hydropower, investment and a trade-treaty update on the agenda after months of strain.
ideas: Repairing ties: after Nepal's PM declined to meet India's Ambassador and the Foreign Secretary's May visit was cancelled, visits by Nepal's Finance Minister and a ruling-party leader began a course correction.
GS2 · India–Nepal
India–Nepal ties show how sustained engagement can repair a relationship after political friction.
Disaster diplomacy builds goodwill: after the August 26 flash flood, India sent humanitarian aid, emergency power support and Bailey bridges, and Nepal's PM thanked India.
GS2 · Neighbourhood First / GS3 · Disaster management
India's quick flood relief to Nepal shows humanitarian assistance as a tool of neighbourhood diplomacy.
Connectivity at the core: roads, railways, air routes and power transmission lines top the agenda.
GS2 · Connectivity / GS3 · Infrastructure
Cross-border connectivity turns geography into shared growth between India and Nepal.
Clean energy as a shared asset: Nepal's large hydropower plans, through run-of-river and storage projects, make power trade central to the partnership.
GS3 · Energy / GS2 · Regional cooperation
Hydropower trade can make Nepal a clean-energy partner for India's grid.

Economic partnership beyond aid: Nepal seeks Indian investment, digitalisation, green manufacturing and tourism, and both sides will discuss updating the trade treaty to cover services, investment protection and profit repatriation.
GS2 · Bilateral agreements
Updating the trade treaty would move India–Nepal ties from aid to investment and services.
keywords: Flood relief and connectivity projects put Neighbourhood First into practice in Nepal.
Using relief to build trust between states
India's flood aid to Nepal is disaster diplomacy that rebuilt goodwill.
Generating power from river flow with little storage
Run-of-river and storage projects underpin Nepal's hydropower ambitions.
Cross-border power trade can integrate South Asia's grids.
examples: Bailey bridges for Nepal after the flood
India's quick relief after the August 26 flash flood
GS4
GS2 · Neighbourhood First · GS3 · Disaster management · GS4 · Compassion in IR
India's flood relief to Nepal shows compassion and strategy working together in neighbourhood diplomacy.
India–Nepal course correction
From snubs to high-level visits within months
GS2 · India and its neighbourhood
India–Nepal ties show patient diplomacy outlasting political friction.
pyqs: China's BRI turning South Asia into a theatre of competition.
How domestic factors shape foreign policy towards a neighbour.
Project Mausam and India's neighbourhood outreach.

trend.t: Neighbourhood questions moved from domestic factors in foreign policy (Sri Lanka, 2013) and the Maldives (2013, 2024) to Sri Lanka's crisis (2022) and China's BRI turning South Asia into a theatre of competition (2026). Hydropower technology came in GS3 (2013).
trend.watch: Small neighbours, with China's role in the background, keep returning. Prepare India's tools: connectivity, energy trade, disaster relief and economic partnership, with Nepal as an example.
focus: Connectivity and energy trade with neighbours
Managing political friction with small neighbours

potential: "Connectivity and clean energy can anchor India's relations with Nepal beyond political cycles." Discuss. (10 marks)

practice.q: "Connectivity and clean energy can anchor India's relations with Nepal beyond political cycles." Discuss.

answer.t: Foreign Secretary Misri's Nepal visit, preparing for PM Balen Shah's India trip, puts roads, railways, power lines and hydropower at the centre after months of friction.

pts.t: Power trade and transit create mutual dependence.
Roads and rail serve citizens on both sides.
Nepal's hydropower can feed India's grid.
Connectivity aids disaster relief.
pts.ex: Bailey bridges after the August flood.

pts.t: Leaders' snubs disrupted engagement.
Past delays bred distrust.
Competing infrastructure offers.
Services and investment not covered.
Complete projects on schedule.
Cover services and investment protection.
Regular high-level exchanges.

answer.t: Roads, rails and power lines can outlast governments; delivering them on time is India's best diplomacy in Nepal.

items.title: NTA overhaul: 5,000 experts empanelled for setting, vetting question papers
items.syllabus: GS2 › Issues relating to education; Statutory and executive bodies; Government policies · GS4 › Probity and integrity in public institutions
items.summary: After the NEET-UG paper leak, the NTA has empanelled thousands of vetted experts and is building a large question bank so papers can be finalised minutes before exams.
ideas: Crisis forced reform: after the NEET-UG paper leak in May, which led to protests and the Education Minister's resignation, the NTA dropped about 600 experts and moved its headquarters.
GS2 · Education governance
Exam leaks erode public trust, forcing institutional overhaul at testing bodies.
Vetting for integrity: experts are empanelled after multi-layer checks, including no links to coaching institutes, and must sign and reaffirm non-disclosure agreements.
GS2 · Institutional reform / GS4 · Integrity
Background checks and confidentiality rules guard against conflicts of interest in exam setting.
Design against leaks: a large question bank lets papers be finalised minutes before an exam, and setters do not know which exam a question is for.
GS2 · Exam reform
A large question bank and late paper assembly reduce the window for leaks.
Technology helps: most NTA exams except NEET are computer-based, and AI-translated material is reviewed by experts.
GS2 · E-governance
Computer-based testing and secure question banks make exams harder to compromise.
keywords: Large pool of pre-vetted questions drawn at random
A large question bank prevents setters from memorising papers.
Personal interest clashing with official duty
Barring experts linked to coaching institutes removes conflicts of interest.
Public trust in an institution's fairness
Exam integrity is central to the credibility of testing institutions.
examples: NTA's post-leak overhaul
Vetted experts, NDAs and a large question bank
GS4
GS2 · Education, institutional reform · GS4 · Probity, conflict of interest
The NTA's overhaul shows how an institution rebuilds trust after a breach through systems, not slogans.
pyqs: Aims of the Public Examination (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024.
potential: Examine the measures needed to restore credibility to India's national entrance examinations. (10 marks)
